title: How Columbia Artists Community Concerts led to A Night at Eddie Condon's
summary: Columbia Artists saw his 1992 concert; he built a story-driven jazz show for their Community Concerts circuit.

blocks.x: This concept of “The Magic of Swing Street,” when did it kind of come together for you?

Well Community — Columbia Artists came to a concert I did in 1992 up at the Emelin Theater up in Westchester. I invited them because I knew that they have probably five or six hundred venues throughout the United States, an organization called Community Concerts. And what they do is, it started out as a classical Columbia Records or Columbia Recordings started it many years ago, 75 or 80 years ago, as an outlet for their artists and what they did was a small community would get up a budget let’s say of $30,000 okay. Community Concerts would go out and say well we can bring you The Kirov Ballet, we can bring you Ed Polcer and his jazz band, we can bring you a concert pianist, we can bring you a circus act, and that will all fit your budget. So that year, in Cut Bank Shelby, Montana, you can have some of the greatest entertainment in the world, and all it’s going to cost you as a person is maybe $20 for the whole concert series. So they get this budget going, and so I knew about Columbia Artists. But I just didn’t want to have just the jazz concert, I felt that it was a perfect opportunity of bringing, in an entertaining way, the music. In other words a little story that went along, so effectively it’s like a mini-show but it’s basically a jazz concert.
